explanations.explanation: Jesus says it plain: 'No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.' That's a short list, friend, and it has exactly one name on it. So I quit trying to guess a date. I just keep my ovens warm and my apron on.

Close, but look at what Jesus says: 'nor the Son, but only the Father.' He puts Himself right there in the line, which tells you how firmly this one belongs to the Father. The answer is the Father alone. Plenty of folks would guess the Son, so you're in good company, baker.
The angels are actually the first ones Jesus rules out: 'not even the angels in heaven.' Think about that, baker. Even the angels in heaven don't have the date. The Father alone knows it.

Noah it is. Jesus says, 'As it was in the days of Noah, so will it be at the coming of the Son of Man.' Out of every picture He could pick, He points back to the days before the flood, when people carried on right up to the day Noah entered the ark. So when He talks about His coming, that's the picture He hands you.

Moses is a big name, and it's easy to reach for him. But Jesus doesn't mention Moses here. He says 'the days of Noah,' and the picture He paints is the time before the flood. Noah's the name that fits this blank.

David is another famous name, so I get why he came to mind. But Jesus doesn't bring him up in this passage. He goes back to 'the days of Noah,' when people carried on with life until the day Noah entered the ark. Noah's the name for this blank.

Jesus says people were 'eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, up to the day Noah entered the ark.' That's everyday life, friend. Meals, weddings, the normal rhythm of things. Jesus puts it right up to the day Noah went in.

Jesus doesn't mention fasting or rain at all. He says they were 'eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage.' That's ordinary life, going on right up to the day Noah entered the ark. Nobody in this passage is praying for rain, friend. They're busy with regular life.

Nothing in this passage has the people building boats. Jesus says they were 'eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage,' right up to the day Noah entered the ark. Only Noah is mentioned going into one. The rest were busy with regular life.

I can see why it feels that way, but Jesus says the opposite. 'They were oblivious until the flood came and swept them all away.' Oblivious means they didn't see it coming. This is a heavy part of the story, friend, so let it sit a moment.

Right, friend. Jesus says, 'they were oblivious until the flood came and swept them all away.' Oblivious means they were unaware of it. It's a heavy picture, so let it sit a moment. Then Jesus says, 'So will it be at the coming of the Son of Man.'

Jesus says it right there: 'Two men will be in the field: one will be taken and the other left.' Same field, two different outcomes. He keeps the picture short and plain. I think the point is that being in the same place doesn't mean the same outcome.

Jesus splits them up. He says 'one will be taken and the other left.' So they're both in the same field, but they don't share the same outcome. If you picked this one, you were thinking of the pair staying together, but the verse separates them.

Jesus doesn't leave them both. He says, 'one will be taken and the other left.' Two men are in the field, and the verse goes one way for one and the other way for the other. That's what the picture is all about.

Yes, baker. 'Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day on which your Lord will come.' Nobody puts a batch in the oven and then wanders off to rearrange the pantry. You stay close, you stay alert, and you keep an eye on the timer. Jesus asks His disciples to do that same watching.

Jesus doesn't say anything about quiet here. He says 'keep watch.' It's about staying alert, not about being silent. If you picked quiet, I get it, because watching can feel like a hush, but the word is watch.

That one's flipped, friend. Jesus doesn't say 'keep away.' He says 'keep watch,' and the reason is that you 'do not know the day on which your Lord will come.' You stay near and stay alert. Walking away from the oven is how cookies end up a little too crispy.

explanations.answer: Kept the thief from breaking in
explanations.explanation: Jesus says that if the homeowner had known, 'he would have kept watch and would not have let his house be broken into.' So the key is knowing the hour and staying alert. The trouble is that nobody gets that hour handed to them. That's the point of the story.

Hiding valuables? Jesus never says that, friend. He says the homeowner 'would have kept watch and would not have let his house be broken into.' Watching is the whole plan. Nobody's stuffing anything under a mattress in this story.

explanations.answer: Left the house for the night
explanations.explanation: Leaving isn't what Jesus says. He says the homeowner 'would have kept watch and would not have let his house be broken into.' He stays and he watches. Walking out the front door is the opposite of watching.

Yes, baker. 'For this reason, you also must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect.' Jesus takes the homeowner picture and points it at His disciples. The reason comes right after the word: an hour you do not expect. Ready is the word, and it's the same word my ovens live by.
Jesus doesn't ask for silence here. He says 'you also must be ready.' The homeowner's story is about being prepared, not about staying quiet. Ready is the word for this blank.

Hiding isn't what Jesus is asking for. He says, 'you also must be ready,' and then gives the reason: 'the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect.' Being ready is about being prepared for that hour, not tucked away somewhere. Ready is the word for this blank.

Jesus says it straight: 'Blessed is that servant whose master finds him doing so when he returns.' Doing what? Giving the others their food at the proper time. It's steady, faithful work, and the master finds him right in the middle of it.

Jesus doesn't call him tested. He says, 'Blessed is that servant whose master finds him doing so when he returns.' The master comes back and finds him giving the others their food at the proper time. Jesus calls that servant blessed, and that's the word for this one.
Nope, friend. The faithful servant isn't replaced. Jesus calls him blessed. Then He adds, 'he will put him in charge of all his possessions.' That's a promotion, not a pink slip.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, 'Truly I tell you, he will put him in charge of all his possessions.' The servant was trusted with the household, and he's trusted with even more. The master finds him doing his job and puts him over everything he owns. Faithful work gets noticed.

It's actually true, friend. Jesus says, 'Truly I tell you, he will put him in charge of all his possessions.' The faithful servant is already in charge of the household, and the master puts him over everything he owns. That's a big reward.

explanations.answer: My master will be away a long time
explanations.explanation: That's his thought, baker. Jesus says the wicked servant 'says in his heart, ‘My master will be away a long time.’' So he expects his master to be gone a long while. Then watch what he does, because Jesus is about to tell us.

explanations.answer: My master is coming back tonight
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what the servant says. Jesus says he 'says in his heart, ‘My master will be away a long time.’' He's expecting a long delay, not a quick return. That's what makes the master's arrival such a surprise to him.

Jesus doesn't have the servant say that. The servant says in his heart, 'My master will be away a long time.' He's thinking about how long the master will be gone. The trust part belongs to the master, who put him in charge of the household.

Not quite, friend. Jesus says the wicked servant 'begins to beat his fellow servants and to eat and drink with drunkards.' That's what Jesus tells us he does. Giving the others their food at the proper time is what the faithful servant does.

Yes, baker, it's False. Jesus says the wicked servant 'begins to beat his fellow servants and to eat and drink with drunkards.' That's what Jesus tells us he does. Giving the others their food at the proper time is what the faithful servant does (Matthew 24:45). He's the one the master finds doing so when he returns (Matthew 24:46).

explanations.answer: On a day the servant does not expect
explanations.explanation: Exactly. Jesus says, 'The master of that servant will come on a day he does not expect and at an hour he does not anticipate.' The servant had told himself his master would be away a long time. Then the master comes on a day he doesn't expect. That's the whole surprise.

explanations.answer: On the very day he promised
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't mention any promised day. He says the master 'will come on a day he does not expect and at an hour he does not anticipate.' So the day catches the servant by surprise. It isn't a day he's expecting.

Jesus doesn't mention any word sent ahead. He says the master 'will come on a day he does not expect and at an hour he does not anticipate.' The master arrives on a day the servant does not expect. That's the part Jesus puts on the table.
